papers.title: CD19-CAR T-cell therapy resets the EBV+ autoreactive B cell repertoire in autoimmune disease
papers.authors: Courtney, Y.; Pandit, M.; van Dam, L. S.; Younis, S.; Rasouli, S.; Zhang, M.; Chaichian, Y.; Parsafar, S.; Lanz, T. V.; Arends, E.; van Kooten, C.; Teng, Y. K. O.; Hagen, M.; Wirsching, A.; Muller, F.; Mackensen, A.; Bozec, A.; Grieshaber-Bouyer, R.; Schett, G.; Robinson, W. H.
papers.abstract: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) reprograms autoreactive B cells into activated antigen-presenting cells that drive pathogenic T- and B-cell responses in autoimmune disease. Whether eliminating these cells contributes to durable remission after CD19 chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy is unknown. Here, using EBV B-cell sequencing (EBV-seq), we profiled EBV+ B cells from patients treated with CD19-CAR T cells (systemic lupus erythematosus, n=6; inflammatory myopathy, n=3; systemic sclerosis, n=3) or rituximab (n=15) and recombinantly expressed their antibodies to define antigen specificity. At baseline, EBV+ B cells were enriched relative to healthy donors, class-switched and hypermutated, expressed the latency III program with heightened antigen-presentation signatures, and encoded autoantibodies. CAR T cells, but not rituximab, depleted EBV+ B cells and shifted the reconstituted repertoire towards IgM+, minimally mutated, largely non-autoreactive cells, consistent with infection of newly generated B cells. After rituximab, EBV+ B cells retained a class-switched, hypermutated and autoreactive with an activated antigen-presenting phenotype. Sustained drug-free remission occurred in 8/12 CAR T-cell-treated versus 0/15 rituximab-treated patients. In vitro, EBV+ B cells resisted anti-CD20 and anti-CD19 antibodies but were killed by CAR T cells and a CD19 T-cell engager. Our findings suggest resetting the EBV+ autoreactive B-cell repertoire contributes to sustained drug-free remission.

papers.title: Decoding antibody-antigen recognition: the BL8 language and its application in calibrating deep learning predictions
papers.authors: Miao, T.; Zhu, R.; Lin, R.; Qian, J.; Feng, Y.; Chen, S.; Wang, Y.; Chen, D.; Wu, Y.; Ying, T.
papers.abstract: Antibodies are central to immunology and therapeutics, and understanding how they recognize antigens is essential to rational drug design. This recognition depends on the interplay of interface geometry, physicochemical interactions, sequence context, and complementarity-determining region (CDR) conformation. However, traditional analyses often oversimplify this complexity, which becomes particularly problematic when evaluating the massive and frequently overconfident structural hypotheses generated by modern deep learning models. Here, we introduce BL8, an interpretable, eight-view structural language that comprehensively parameterizes interfaces across topology, shape, interaction, CDR conformation, flexibility, interfacial area, amino-acid-pair composition, and sequence background. Using 15,396 experimental interface records from the Structural Antibody Database (SAbDab), we built a fixed reference atlas containing 1,498 discrete BL8 signatures. The atlas shows that natural interfaces occupy a diverse, long-tailed structural space in which similar geometric scaffolds can be associated with different chemical and sequence features. Furthermore, we projected 28,501 predicted complexes involving programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1), the SARS-CoV-2 receptor-binding domain (RBD), and programmed cell death protein 1 (PD-1), generated using AlphaFold 3 (AF3), Protenix-v2, and OpenDDE, into the reference space. Acting as a robust underlying calibration layer, BL8 successfully decoupled physical viability from native confidence illusions, revealing cross-target hallucinations and filtering out 15.3% to 20.1% of highly deceptive false-positive predictions. Crucially, by benchmarking distinct generative behaviors across models, it enabled the extraction of highly reliable, multi-model consensus out-of-distribution binding paradigms. Together, BL8 bridges foundational biophysics with large-scale computational predictions, providing an essential benchmarking framework for discovering novel mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

papers.title: JAK1/2 Inhibition Restores Tissue Integrity by Rewiring Type 1/2 Immunity Toward Targetable IL-17 Responses
papers.authors: Jin, R.; Strobl, K.; Artner-Gent, L.; Tuechler, J.; Gladkova, M.; Mann, U.; Farlik, M.; Barozzi, I.; Sibilia, M.; Bauer, T.
papers.abstract: Effective immune responses require coordinated communication between immune and epithelial cells to eliminate pathogens while limiting tissue damage. Disruption of this balance drives chronic inflammation and progressive tissue destruction. The Janus kinase (JAK) pathway coordinates cytokine signaling across these compartments and has emerged as a therapeutic target in inflammatory diseases. However, the consequences of JAK inhibition within a complex inflammatory environment remain incompletely understood. Here, we dissect the molecular, cellular, immunological and phenotypical effects of topical JAK1/2 inhibition in a chronic model of tissue-destructive skin inflammation driven by barrier dysfunction and bacterial superinfection. Single-cell transcriptomics and functional profiling revealed that JAK1/2 blockade selectively suppressed pathogenic CD8 T cells and their IFN-{gamma} production while shifting Th2-polarized CD4 T cells toward a Th17 phenotype, preserving type 3 immunity consisting of IL-17A-producing {gamma}{delta}-T cells and neutrophil responses. This immune rebalancing occurs rapidly and concomitantly with the restoration of epithelial barrier integrity through tight junction reinforcement, followed by recovery of antimicrobial defenses and reduced bacterial burden. Combination of JAK1/2 and IL-17A blockade further improved tissue homeostasis by targeting residual type 3-driven pathology. Thus, JAK1/2 inhibition acts as selective immunomodulator rather than a broad immunosuppressant, targeting pathogenic type 1/2 responses while preserving type-3-associated antimicrobial defense programs. These findings reveal how JAK1/2 inhibition coordinates immune rebalancing with epithelial repair and support its therapeutic potential in chronic type 1/2-driven inflammatory disease, while identifying residual IL-17A-mediated pathology as a target for combination therapy.

papers.title: A minimal two-residue C-terminal truncation of AID in adult-onset hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2)
papers.authors: Green, K.; Rovsing, A. B.; Terczynska-Dyla, E.; Jensen, L.; Machalica, K.; Wolff, J. H.; Westerberg, L.; Larsen, C. S.; Lin, L.; Mikkelsen, J. G.; Jensen, J. M. B.; Degn, S. E.
papers.abstract: Activation-induced cytidine deaminase (AID), encoded by AICDA, facilitates class-switch recombination (CSR) and somatic hypermutation (SHM) in activated B cells. Loss of AID function causes hyper-IgM syndrome type 2 (HIGM2). While typically autosomal recessive, three C-terminal truncation variants have been reported to act in autosomal dominant manner. We describe a novel heterozygous AICDA nonsense variant, c.589G>T (p.G197*), that truncates the final two C-terminal residues of AID and results in adult-onset HIGM2. Single-cell sequencing of primary patient B cells revealed a complete block in CSR and a [~]10-fold reduction in SHM. AICDA mRNA expression was balanced between wild-type and variant alleles, yet AID protein abundance was reduced to [~]56% with normal subcellular localization. Remarkably, inducible germinal center (iGB) cultures restored CSR in purified naive patient B cells. CRISPR-Cas9 editing of healthy donor B cells confirmed that the iGB platform can rescue B cells harboring heterozygous, but not homozygous, AICDA variants. These results demonstrate that even a two-amino-acid truncation at the AID C-terminus is sufficient to disrupt its function and cause HIGM2.

papers.title: Gene regulatory logic underlying the differentiation of mixed lineages in human thymic epithelial cells
papers.authors: Prabakar, R. K.; Chapin, S. R.; Lin, Y.; Staklinski, S. J.; Netz, D. M.; Lapine, M. E.; Pruss, D.; Cvetanovic, T.; Carcy, S. L.; Torres, J.; Grosh, A.; Kiedrowski, A. J.; Pass, H. I.; Mosca, R.; Regan, C.; Preall, J.; Siepel, A.; Meyer, H. V.
papers.abstract: The thymus enacts central tolerance through thymic (TECs), which present self-antigens to developing T cells self-reactive cells, preventing autoimmunity. Human TECs include populations that express lineage-committed programs corresponding to distinct peripheral tissues, yet how they acquire these programs and whether these TEC subpopulations are genetically related and conserved in mice remain unknown. Using matched single-cell gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility profiling of 126,687 human TECs, we identified 17 TEC subsets defined by their distinct expression profiles of 1,843 cell type restricted-antigens (CRAs) from 48 peripheral cell types. With a new phylogenetic reconstruction method, we show that lineage-committed TECs share a common ancestor, retain a thymus-specific mixed identity through co-expression of multiple CRA signatures, and are specified by coordinated activator and repressor regulons. We also identified a basement-membrane-collagen-rich state (BMC-TECs) with progenitor-like properties. Finally, mouse TECs shared the regulatory strategy but conserved few master transcription-factor drivers. This study mechanistically characterizes human TEC subpopulations and reveals the gene regulatory logic that leads to their distinct diversification and mixed identities in humans and mice.
